content: Sudden cardiac arrest (SCA), also referred to as sudden cardiac death, occurs when the heart abruptly and unexpectedly ceases to beat. When this happens, blood flow to the brain and other vital organs is immediately halted. Without prompt treatment, SCA is almost always fatal within minutes. The heart relies on an internal electrical system to regulate its rhythm. Disruptions in this electrical system can lead to abnormal heart rhythms, known as arrhythmias. Arrhythmias can cause the heart to beat too quickly, too slowly, or to stop beating altogether. SCA occurs when an arrhythmia causes the heart to stop beating entirely. It is important to note that SCA is distinct from a heart attack. A heart attack is caused by a blockage in blood flow to a portion of the heart muscle. During a heart attack, the heart typically does not stop beating suddenly. However, SCA can occur during the recovery phase of a heart attack. Individuals with heart disease are at an increased risk of experiencing SCA, but the majority of SCAs occur in people who appear healthy and have no known heart disease or other risk factors. The prognosis for SCA is grim, with 95% of individuals who experience it dying, most within minutes. However, rapid intervention using a defibrillator—a device that delivers an electrical shock to the heart—can be life-saving. Automated external defibrillators (AEDs), which are commonly available in public spaces such as airports and office buildings, can be used to save the lives of individuals experiencing SCA.
